title: Good practices for estimating area and assessing accuracy of land change
relevance: The governing protocol for everything we report: stratified probability sampling, unbiased area estimation from the reference sample rather than pixel counting, and confidence intervals on both accuracy and area. Directly applicable to our ~250-point interpretation - it dictates sample allocation, the error-matrix-to-area estimator, and the requirement that our canopy-fraction numbers (30/35/38%) be reported as sample-based estimates with CIs, not as map pixel counts. Note the caution: it assumes the reference is correct, which finding 3 (15-17% inter-reference disagreement) says ours is not - so pair it with Foody 2010 and Stehman & Foody 2019.

title: Making better use of accuracy data in land change studies: Estimating accuracy and area and quantifying uncertainty using stratified estimation
relevance: Gives the stratified estimator worked end-to-end, including the variance formulas needed for CIs on class area. This is the paper that converts our per-year confusion counts into a defensible canopy-area estimate with uncertainty, and shows that map-based area and sample-based area routinely differ by more than the effect we are chasing. Use it to decide whether our 30 vs 35 vs 38% canopy-fraction spread is even separable given sample size.

title: Key issues in rigorous accuracy assessment of land cover products
relevance: The current synthesis of good practice across sampling design, response design, and analysis, and explicitly flags imperfect reference data as an under-treated problem - the exact position we are in. Tells us what must be documented for reproducibility, which is the checklist our accuracy reporting should be written against. Its treatment of response design directly informs Search 14's interpretation protocol.

title: Estimating area and map accuracy for stratified random sampling when the strata are different from the map classes
relevance: Answers our stratification question head-on: it is legitimate to stratify on something other than the map classes - including a stratification built from reference products - provided you use the estimators given here, which keep the area and accuracy estimates unbiased while inflating variance relative to map-based strata. This licenses the design we want, stratifying by CHM height band and by C-CAP/NDVI agreement-vs-disagreement, and supplies the exact overall/user's/producer's accuracy and standard-error formulas for that case. Without this paper our proposed reference-based stratification would be indefensible.

title: Optimizing sample size allocation to strata for estimating area and map accuracy
relevance: Provides an objective allocation rule (and spreadsheet) that minimizes the summed variance of user's accuracy, producer's accuracy, and area for a target class, instead of the usual ad hoc proportional or equal allocation. This is how we split ~250 points across CHM height bands so the 5-15 m band - which holds 53% of our missed pixels - gets enough samples to estimate its recall precisely rather than being swamped by the tall-canopy majority. Directly determines the design of the interpretation run.

title: Choosing a sample size allocation to strata based on trade-offs in precision when estimating accuracy and area of a rare class from a stratified sample
relevance: Extends the allocation problem to rare classes and makes the trade-offs explicit: an allocation that sharpens one estimate degrades another, so the design must state which estimate it is optimizing. Relevant because our decision-critical strata (short trees under 5 m, disagreement pixels) are rare relative to the city, and a proportional 250-point sample would put only a handful of points in them. Use with Wagner & Stehman 2015 to justify deliberately over-sampling the short-canopy and disagreement strata.

authors: Radoux, J., Waldner, F. & Bogaert, P.
title: How response designs and class proportions affect the accuracy of validation data
relevance: Quantifies error introduced by the response design itself - the interpreter's labeling procedure - and shows it grows with landscape heterogeneity and with mixed class proportions inside the sampling unit, which is exactly the fragmented residential canopy of Edmonds. Its adaptive scheme spends little effort on unambiguous points and concentrates interpretation on ambiguous ones, cutting effort 50-75% at equal accuracy; that is a concrete design for handling our 'unsure' responses rather than discarding them. Implies our validation points are themselves noisy, reinforcing finding 3 that reference disagreement is partly reference error, not map error.

title: Death to Kappa: birth of quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement for accuracy assessment
relevance: Replaces kappa with quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement, which decompose a confusion matrix into 'wrong amount' versus 'right amount, wrong place'. This is the right summary for our 15-17% inter-reference disagreement: it tells us whether NDVI and C-CAP disagree about how much canopy exists or about where it is, which are different problems with different fixes. Also the correct frame for the finding that IoU 0.49-0.76 does not move recall - allocation error can swing while quantity error stays fixed.
